title: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Regions sharing many allied species will also share some identical species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Wherever two regions, however distant, contain many closely allied or representative species, they will also contain some identical species and many doubtful forms ranked variously as species or varieties, showing past migration between them.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: And it will, I believe, be universally found to be true, that wherever in two regions, let them be ever so distant, many closely allied or representative species occur, there will likewise be found some identical species

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification”. Scope: pairs of geographic regions with related biotas

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-16: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.80

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The universal prediction has a clear counterexample criterion and broad occurrence and phylogenetic data exist. Taxonomic uncertainty and sampling incompleteness reduce confidence but can be modeled.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across pairs of regions, quantify counts of close phylogenetic replacements and test whether those counts predict shared species after controlling for area, distance and sampling. A reliably positive association supports the prediction; region pairs with many allied forms but no shared species refute its universal wording.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Unequal inventory effort creates false absences.

Species concepts and doubtful forms vary among taxonomic authorities.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.88
operationalizability: 0.86
data adequacy: 0.72
analysis feasibility: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Shared species, close relatives and nomenclatural borderline cases can be counted from public checklists and trees, so the pattern is operational for vertebrates and seed plants. The universal wording is only as strong as taxonomic practice, which uses the same gaps the claim is about. The analysis is feasible at bioregion scale, with serious circularity around how species and varieties are ranked.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across pairs of bioregions, count shared species, sister or congeneric pairs, and taxa with unstable species-versus-variety rank, then test whether regions rich in allied pairs also share some identical species and more borderline taxa. The claim is confirmed if that joint pattern is nearly general after controlling for region size and survey effort, and refuted if many region pairs have numerous allied species and no shared species.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A few very widespread species can create shared-species counts without any special history of migration.

Taxonomists already split and lump borderline forms most actively where regions share related biotas, so 'doubtful forms' partly reflect effort.

Survey effort and species concepts differ sharply between regions, which can manufacture or hide the predicted association.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.5
data existence: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.65
